chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far Al-Qurashi Al-Razzaz Al-Kufi narrated to me from his uncle Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Salih ibn Uqbah, from Bashir al-Dahhan, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Sometimes I miss the Hajj, so I go to perform 'Arfah (stand in devotion) near the grave of al-Husayn (peace be upon him).' He said, 'Well done, O Bashir! Whoever of the believers visits the grave of al-Husayn (peace be upon him), knowing his right, on a day other than an Eid, Allah will record for him twenty Hajj, twenty Umrah (purified and accepted), and twenty battles with a Messenger Prophet or a Just Imam.'
And whoever visits him on an Eid day, Allah will record for him one hundred Hajj, one hundred Umrah, and one hundred battles with a Messenger Prophet or a Just Imam.

And whoever visits him on the Day of 'Arafah, knowing his right, Allah will record for him one thousand accepted Hajj and one thousand Umrah, and one thousand battles with a Messenger Prophet or a Just Imam.

I said to him, 'And how can I have something better than the standing (at 'Arafah)?' He looked at me as if slightly angry, then said, 'O Bashir! Indeed, when the believer visits the grave of al-Husayn (peace be upon him) on the Day of 'Arafah, and performs Ghusl in the Euphrates, then turns towards it, Allah will record for him, with every step, a complete Hajj with all its rituals.'
And I do not know him except that he said, 'And a battle.'
ai.seo_question: What are the rewards for visiting Imam Husain's grave on the Day of Arafah?
ai.summary: Compiled by Ibn Qulawayh in *Kamil al-Ziyarat*, this hadith establishes the grave of Imam al-Husayn (a.s.) as a spiritual substitute for the Prophet’s presence, linking the pilgrim’s devotion directly to the merits of Hajj and Ghazw. The specific emphasis on the Day of 'Arafah highlights the theological concept of *I'tiraf* (acknowledgment of right), where the visitor’s recognition of the Imam’s status multiplies the reward exponentially, equating each step to a full pilgrimage. This tradition underscores the Shia view that Ziyarah is not merely a visit but a participatory act of worship that mirrors the rituals of the Kaaba.
